title: VASTRA: Efficient Agentic Top-K Interactive Video Analysis
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable natural language video retrieval, bypassing traditional hand-engineered pipelines. Integrating agentic reasoning frameworks (e.g., ReAct) further advances this paradigm by allowing models to dynamically inspect video content rather than relying on a single visual pass. Applying this pattern naively to video retrieval inherits problems that video systems cannot afford: results vary from run to run under identical conditions, and cost and latency scale with every reasoning step the agent takes rather than with the work the query actually requires. We present VASTRA, an agentic video retrieval system whose execution is dictated by query complexity rather than an open-ended reasoning loop: cheap, reliably answerable queries are ranked directly from pre-ingested summaries, while harder queries trigger targeted verification only where relevance is genuinely uncertain. This keeps control flow external to the model rather than latent in a growing chain of thought, establishing deterministic control flow by construction and end-to-end rank reproducibility under greedy serving. Across 40 benchmark queries, VASTRA exposes explicit presets: VASTRA-Fast runs 12.2x faster (4.2 s vs. 51.2 s) and 10.4x cheaper ($0.0044 vs. $0.0458) than best performing ReAct agent at a 5.0-point mAP reduction, while VASTRA-Max matches peak ReAct agent accuracy (0.653 vs. 0.649 mAP) at comparable latency, trading higher spend ($0.1022 vs. $0.0458) for zero run-to-run variance.

title: Beyond Foreign-Key Connectivity: Semantic Relationship Representation for Relational Deep Learning
summary:
Relational databases encode information through tables and primary--foreign key constraints. Although recent Relational Deep Learning (RDL) approaches represent these databases as heterogeneous graphs, a foreign-key connection primarily specifies structural connectivity between records. Its semantic interpretation may involve additional information that is not explicitly represented by connectivity alone.
  This paper introduces a conceptual framework for constructing relationship-aware representations from relational databases. The framework distinguishes three complementary aspects: (i) schema-defined relationship semantics, including endpoint types and foreign-key roles; (ii) association entities and explicitly available relationship-level attributes; and (iii) contextual information describing the temporal and structural circumstances of a connection.
  We formulate a Relationship Representation Construction (RRC) protocol that maps relational schema elements and database records to node representations, relationship descriptors, and contextual representations. A key principle of the protocol is semantic ownership: attributes are assigned to records, relationships, or context according to their meaning, rather than merely their physical location in a database table. Ambiguous attributes are not automatically promoted to relationship features.
  The resulting representations can be incorporated into existing relational graph learning architectures through relationship-conditioned message passing. The proposed framework is complementary to recent work on relational message passing, graph transformers, and task-dependent graph construction. We discuss its conceptual foundations, illustrate the construction protocol using a multi-table database, and identify research questions and empirical evaluations required to establish its potential benefits.

title: Auriga: Harness-Governed LLM Agents for Effective Throughput Optimization in Execute-Order-Validate Permissioned Blockchains
summary: Effective throughput, the product of raw throughput and transaction success rate, determines the useful capacity of Execute-Order-Validate blockchains such as Hyperledger Fabric. Most prior work either tunes configurations to raise raw throughput, requiring many costly redeployments, or controls conflicts to raise the success rate, repairing them only after execution with kernel modifications. The few joint approaches tune only a small set of parameters and still rely on kernel changes to resolve conflicts. To address these challenges, we present Auriga, a non-invasive framework that jointly optimizes both factors through sample-efficient LLM-guided configuration search and pre-execution conflict prevention. A harness-governed multi-agent architecture coordinates LLM agents for parameter exploration, saturation-aware evaluation, and experience consolidation, with the harness controlling tool and memory access and retaining termination authority. For transaction scheduling, an LLM extracts symbolic AST templates from smart contracts offline. At runtime, the scheduler predicts read-write sets without executing them and partitions transactions into conflict-free groups. Across three benchmarks and conflict rates up to 70%, Auriga improves effective throughput by up to 6.0 times over default Fabric and 2.0 times over the strongest baseline. The tuning agent also discovers undocumented parameter dependencies, and ablation studies show the independent contributions of both subsystems.

title: VecDBLens: An Evaluatology-Based Framework for Vector Database Diagnosis
summary: Vector databases are increasingly deployed as retrieval pipelines in which representation, indexing, and query-time execution jointly determine accuracy, throughput, and cost. Existing vector database evaluations primarily focus on indexing while treating embeddings as fixed inputs and ignoring the role of query-time execution, making it difficult to decide whether a bottleneck should be addressed by changing the embedding model, the index, or the query-processing functions. To address the above limitation, we introduce VecDBLens, an Evaluatology-based framework that treats the function under diagnosis as an evaluated object and all remaining dataset, workload, parameter, and runtime factors as matched evaluation conditions. VecDBLens attributes performance differences to individual evaluated objects through comparisons under matched evaluation conditions, summarizing their performance and stability across multiple datasets and workloads. It further analyzes interactions among objects using analysis of variance (ANOVA), thereby turning vector database benchmarking from leaderboard ranking into a reproducible diagnostic procedure. VecDBLens reveals two key insights. First, retrieval performance is fundamentally upper-bounded by embedding quality, revealing that many apparent indexing failures are therefore representation-side limitations. Second, stronger index parameterization is not always beneficial: overly aggressive configurations can reshape neighborhood topology and cause recall regression. These results challenge the common practice of evaluating vector databases primarily through indexing and show that real-world limitations arise from constraints across retrieval functions rather than any single function alone. VecDBLens provides a principled basis for identifying the true performance drivers of vector databases and for guiding their design in practical applications.

title: Beyond Symmetry: Asymmetric Matching with Transformers for Collective Entity Resolution
summary: A core assumption of entity resolution (ER) is its symmetric nature, which rests on a principle so self-evident it borders on tautology: if a refers to the same object as b, then b must also refer to the same object as a. However, this global property of symmetry does not necessarily extend to each of the complex decision processes within ER systems. In cases involving vague or ambiguous information, enforcing symmetry can be detrimental to performance, an issue exemplified by the ``bad triplet problem''. This paper investigates the effects of input-order asymmetry within a collective ER framework that integrates distinct matching and clustering stages. The input order-aware matching stage utilizes pre-trained transformers to explicitly model and exploit asymmetry, making it possible to evaluate its effect on clustering performance across multiple benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate that asymmetry is not only measurable but also introduces a significant skew in the final entity clusters, highlighting the need to re-evaluate supervised training methodologies for matchers, particularly the development of direction-aware training paradigms that can preserve, rather than neutralize, the inherent asymmetry in matching tasks.

title: Probe-Based Routing for Join Optimizer Selection
summary: In optimizers that choose a join-order solver by a size rule, join ordering is an algorithm-selection problem, because dynamic programming (DP), genetic search (GEQO), and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) each win on different queries. PostgreSQL nevertheless chooses among them by relation count alone, although queries with the same relation count can favor different solvers. This paper introduces two landscape features that a probe computes from random join orders in microseconds per query. The tail spacing $α$ describes how the costs of the best sampled orders are spaced, and the crossover surprise $θ$ describes how far the cost of a crossover child deviates from the mean cost of its parents. The router clusters training queries by these features and the relation count, assigns a solver to every cluster that this solver wins in total end-to-end time by a margin, and leaves all other queries to PostgreSQL's default rule. On JOB and IMDb-CEB, the router lowers mean end-to-end time relative to the default rule, and on IMDb-CEB the probe features nearly double the gain obtained from the relation count alone, so they carry information about the queries that the relation count lacks.

title: Optimal-Time Independent Subset Sampling over Acyclic Joins
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables
summary: Join results can greatly exceed their inputs even when applications need only a small random subset. We study sampling that includes each result independently with a prescribed probability given by the product of its input-tuple weights (PRODUCT). For fixed full acyclic joins with static weights, we achieve input-linear preprocessing and index space together with output-linear expected sampling work, eliminating logarithmic factors from previous bounds. A shared join-tree index supports weighted draws over the entire join and locates high-probability results. Direct Bernoulli trials handle high-probability results, allowing Poisson thinning to generate the remaining independent inclusion decisions with bounded overhead. Our exact sampler uses expected $O(N)$ preprocessing, $O(N)$ index space, and expected $O(1+mμ)$ time per call including output construction. Here $N$ is the input size, $m$ counts relation occurrences, and $μ$ is the expected sample size. The guarantees hold on a real random-access machine with unit-cost exact arithmetic and logarithms, continuous uniform randomness, and expected-time hashing. The time bounds are optimal, matching input reading and explicit output writing. Our floating-point prototype has lower sampling latency than the fastest applicable baseline in 17 of 18 PRODUCT settings on three queries over the STATS benchmark. Construction savings on large joins can offset indexed materialization's faster sampling over a limited number of calls. On a real-data path at $μ=100$, our sampler achieves a $20.5\times$ speedup over indexed materialization for construction plus 300 calls, measured after common data preparation and loading.

title: Towards Unified File Management for Data Lakehouse Systems
comment: Submitted to ICDE 2027
summary: Data lakehouse systems have garnered widespread adoption, yet their metadata management systems face a fundamental architectural dilemma. File-based OTFs (Open Table Formats) scale well, but suffer from metadata bloat, high commit latencies, the absence of multi-table transactions, and unsafe garbage collection. On the other hand, catalogs relying entirely on a transactional database incur severe scalability bottlenecks due to analytic file-level metadata. To reconcile this tension, we present Raven, an operational catalog that stores transactional metadata within a database while offloading analytical metadata to underlying OTF structures. Based on this hybrid architecture, Raven introduces an extended Merge-on-Read (MoR) mechanism to reduce commit latency and mitigate metadata bloat, alongside multi-table transactions under snapshot isolation. Furthermore, Raven unifies core data lakehouse semantics including versioning and reference tracking under an extensible ER (Entity-Relationship) metadata model, enabling safe global garbage collection across diverse types of assets. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that Raven substantially reduces commit latency and metadata bloat when integrated with Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake, maintains a catalog storage footprint orders of magnitude smaller than database-only systems like DuckLake, and achieves scalable garbage collection with minimal disruption.

title: REWEAVE: Online Learning for Workload-Adaptive HNSW Indexes
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Full version with appendix
summary:
Vector databases rely on Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) indexes for similarity search, but a graph built from data alone can be poorly matched to a skewed or changing query workload. We present REWEAVE (Reward-Guided Rewiring of Vector Graphs), an online index-maintenance method that learns edge utility from query feedback and periodically rewires the bottom layer within the original per-node degree cap. The method supports sparse exact-neighbor feedback combined with self-labels, and standard HNSW serving without learning overhead once adaptation is disabled.
  Under explicit assumptions we prove value-estimation and graph-stabilization guarantees. Under stationary skew, REWEAVE improves held-out recall by up to 23.3 percentage points over HNSW. In comparisons with query-aware baselines on up to 100M vectors, it achieves up to 3.3x NGFix's query throughput at recall@100 of 0.80. On Amazon-ESCI with query drift, it increases stream recall@100 from 0.745 to 0.979 with 34% fewer search distance computations than frozen HNSW. These results illustrate the potential to improve retrieval quality and reduce search effort within an existing graph-degree budget, while incurring additional work during adaptation.

title: Calibrated Early Termination with Bounded Optimality Gaps for Constrained Vector Search
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Code available at https://github.com/zhangshea/CaST
summary: Vector search over learned embeddings is the retrieval layer of recommendation and retrieval-augmented generation, and many applications cap how many answer items one category may contribute. Graph indexes answer a query by best-first traversal, and where it stops determines its cost and whether its answer is exact. We study early termination for such constrained $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) queries, with plain $k$-NN as a special case, and seek the cheapest stopping rule whose answer is exact with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$. Learned early-termination methods instead target average recall, which does not guarantee exact answers. Multiple testing can calibrate any parameterized stopping rule to our target, but it cannot tell how much a better rule with the same risk and observations would save. Answering this needs a lower bound on the optimum of a rule family too large to enumerate, valid for the query population. Our key idea is to declare the observations a rule may use and to consider every rule monotone in them. Risk-constrained stopping then becomes a linear program over an order polytope, whose Lagrangian minimizers form a nested chain of staircase rules computed exactly by dynamic programming. Fixed-sequence binomial tests along this chain calibrate our rule, CaST, whose failure probability is at most $\varepsilon$ with confidence $1-δ$. Lagrangian weak duality bounds the optimum of the declared class from below at all risk levels at once, without a union bound over the rules. On two datasets of one million items each, CaST replayed on logged searches costs at most 1.132 times the class optimum for risk levels from 0.03 to 0.10, at 95% joint confidence per setting. Larger savings thus need a rule outside the class. At a common risk target on held-out queries, CaST is faster than every other calibrated rule we time, which take 4.8% to 45.5% more mean time.

title: HyperPage: Learned Page Layouts for Disk-Resident Graph Vector Indexes
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Code available at: https://github.com/zhangshea/HyperPage
summary: Disk-resident graph indexes such as DiskANN store each vector with its graph edges as one record on SSD pages. A search needs the page of every record it expands, so its page reads depend on the page layout, that is, which records share a page. Search agents trained with reinforcement learning query one such index run after run, and every graph traversal can be logged with the records it expands. We therefore use the logs of a finished run to lay out the index for a declared memory budget, so later runs read fewer pages. In contrast, existing layouts such as Starling and MARGO are computed from the graph and vectors and use no logs. Learning a layout from logs is challenging, because the logs must stay valid under every layout, the saving depends on what the budget caches, and the best layout is NP-hard to find. Our key observation is that DiskANN-style search routes on in-memory codes and the records it expands, never on their page-mates. As a result, the logged traversals price every layout by replay, and cached records add no page reads. Accordingly, we propose HyperPage, which first builds layouts for the declared budget on the logged traversals of uncached records. It then selects one layout, together with the budget split between hot records and a page cache, by replaying validation steps. In addition, a Lagrangian lower bound shows how far a layout may be from the optimum. We learn from one Search-R1 agent run and test on a later run with a different reward, over 1M and 21M passages. Across seven cache budgets, HyperPage reads 5.2% to 21.2% fewer pages than MARGO, and no compared layout reads fewer. The advantage is largest when the cache is small. For example, at 1% of the 1M index, MARGO needs nearly 3 times the budget to read as few pages. On the 21M index, HyperPage also cuts search time per step by up to 10.4%. The saving holds for a second agent model and a second corpus.

title: Privacy-Preserving Range Counting over Local Graph Statistics
summary: Range counting over vertex statistics supports contact analysis, community profiling, and reputation screening. However, releasing exact range counts can disclose sensitive edges to an adversary with background knowledge. We study this problem under edge local differential privacy (edge LDP), where each vertex randomizes its report before sending it to an untrusted curator. We develop a layered framework that connects statistic estimation, direct range estimation, and adaptive estimator selection. Statistic-estimation methods provide complementary scalar estimators with explicit loss analyses, while indicator-estimation methods privatize range indicators directly. We next propose Bounded Conditional Range Inversion (BCRI), which derives unbiased range estimates from reusable bounded geometric reports through an explicit local inverse. Its boundary-conditioned estimator achieves no larger expected L2 loss than the unbounded inverse, and histogram preprocessing supports constant-time queries. The same reports also provide a nonnegative, unbiased variance estimate for every answer. At the center of the framework, Adaptive Estimator Selection (AES) privately predicts bias, variance, and covariance to combine BCRI with a conditional estimator from the same transcript. Experiments on diverse real-world graph tasks demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, and workload scalability of the proposed framework.

title: Authenticated Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in Outsourced Vector Databases
summary: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search has become a fundamental query primitive in modern vector databases for managing large-scale embedding data. To support growing vector collections, organizations increasingly outsource database management and query processing to third-party clouds. However, untrusted service providers may return suboptimal or fabricated results, posing a serious threat to ANN search integrity. Existing authenticated ANN approaches face substantial scalability challenges. They typically require transmitting high-dimensional vectors for distance verification and rely on topology-agnostic authentication structures, resulting in excessive communication and verification overhead. In this paper, we propose VIDA, a novel and efficient scheme for authenticated graph-based ANN search. VIDA replaces raw vector transmission with compact vector commitments and employs an aggregated Inner Product Argument to efficiently verify multiple distance computations. Furthermore, we introduce MeST, a topology-aware authenticated data structure that aligns authentication paths with graph traversal, significantly reducing structural proof overhead. Additionally, we design a quantization-aware authentication strategy that exploits distance bounds for pruning, reducing the number of exact distances requiring cryptographic authentication. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed schemes substantially improve the efficiency of authenticated ANN search, achieving up to a $6.6\times$ speedup in end-to-end latency and reducing data transfer time by up to 99.2% compared with state-of-the-art methods.

title: [Experiment, Analysis, and Benchmark] How well do LLMs comprehend and design relational database schemata?
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for database tasks, yet most work, such as Text2SQL, assumes that the relational schema already exists. We ask whether LLMs can design a schema from natural language requirements (Text2Schema), verbalize an existing schema (Schema2Text), and preserve its structure through a Schema-to-Text-to-Schema round trip. We present SchemaBridge, a benchmark of 902 schemata from three collections, stratified by size and constraint complexity, that scores fidelity separately for tables, attributes, domain (data types and nullability), entity, and referential integrity. Evaluating six open-weight and proprietary LLMs, we find that: (i) human-written requirements under-specify schemata, with no model exceeding 0.27 referential integrity F1; (ii) LLM-generated descriptions carry far more structure when explicitly asked to be complete, raising GPT-5.4-mini's referential F1 on SchemaBench from 0.228 to 0.909, even as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore decrease; (iii) controlled experiments show that both constructor and describer choices influence round-trip fidelity under fixed settings; and (iv) masked schema experiments show that structural cues support recovery of keys and relationships, while joint data-type and nullability information is poorly retained through verbalization.
  Code and data are available at https://github.com/iamsriom/SchemaBridge

title: FlinkEval: A Synthetic Corpus for Evaluating Natural Language Interfaces to Streaming SQL
comment: 17 pages
summary: Existing natural-language-to-SQL benchmarks primarily evaluate queries over bounded relational data, leaving streaming semantics underexplored. We introduce FlinkEval, an execution-grounded synthetic benchmark comprising 3,903 question--SQL pairs across 45 industry domains and 45 semantic labels. We create diverse schemas and domain-plausible, temporally consistent data through iterative generation and validation. SQL patterns collected from the human-written NL2SQL pairs and vendor documentation drive quota-balanced generation, and execution with a repair loop on Confluent Cloud Apache Flink produces reference queries covering windowing, temporal joins, pattern matching, nested types, and data manipulation. The corpus includes paired schema-explicit and business-language requests, with annotations for analysis by query pattern, complexity, and execution mode. A seven-level Question Specification Ladder examines semantics-preserving reformulation and underspecified requests augmented with oracle-derived clues. Baseline evaluations combine execution outcomes with adjudicated LLM judgments, revealing challenges in pattern composition and request specification.

title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables, 6 algorithms
summary:
As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle.
  We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not.
  On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

title: An Adaptive Quantum Search Framework under Unknown Solution-density: Minimizing Expected Queries to the First Solution
summary: Grover's algorithm provides a mathematically optimal quadratic speedup for unstructured search, yet its standard formulation relies on a critical prerequisite: prior knowledge of the target solution count to determine the number of algorithm iterations. Although numerous strategies have been developed to identify or bypass this parameter, comparing them directly is nontrivial. This study investigates and computationally optimizes 3 prominent frameworks: Boyer-Brassard-Hoyer-Tapp, Fixed-Point search, and Density Estimation Methods. Density-specific benchmarks select the best tested method and configuration to minimize expected first-solution queries under 2 initialization-cost conventions. To translate these theoretical benchmarks into practical utility, a hybrid quantum-classical adaptive framework integrating Hill-climbing-assisted Grover Adaptive Search with state-space density estimation modeled via the Wang-Landau algorithm is proposed as a potential use-case. This implementation operates directly on the optimized query methods established earlier. Analytical models support the approach; ideal simulations show 18.8%-63.4% lower mean accumulated query costs than the tested randomized and fixed-point baselines.

title: RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION FOR SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS: A REVIEW OF RETRIEVAL, QUESTION ANSWERING, SUMMARIZATION …
summary: The growth of literature is happening faster, making it hard for researchers to find the information they need. They have to look through a lot of things to get the evidence and put together what they find from different studies and make sure their knowledge is accurate. Large Language Models are good for natural language understanding and generation, but they depend on static knowledge, which leads to hallucinations, outdated information and limited transparency in the research domain. One way to solve this problem is the use of Retrieval Augmented Generation. It integrates external knowledge with LLMs to produce evidence for Scientific Questions and Document Summarization. It explores the current improvements in retrieval architectures, including adaptive, hierarchical, graph-based and self-improving strategies, with their applications in literature retrieval, multi-document reasoning and knowledge synthesis. This review discusses evaluation frameworks and benchmark datasets used to assess retrieval quality, citation grounding, answer reliability and faithfulness to the retrieved evidence. In addition, it also identifies current challenges related to retrieval scalability, long-context reasoning, multi-modal research, standardized data evaluation and computational efficiency. Unlike existing surveys that explore individual aspects of RAG, this review uses a unified framework that integrates retrieval architectures, research applications, and evaluation methodologies. It also provides a direction toward trustworthy, scalable and evidence-grounded knowledge systems.

title: Ensemble learning-based ecological speed optimization approach for plug-in hybrid electric vehicles with integrated energy consumption and battery aging
summary: Both energy consumption and battery lifespan of plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) are significantly affected by driving speed. However, precise optimization of ecological velocity remains challenging due to the absence of established relationships that reflect the influence of driving state on both energy consumption and battery aging. To address this issue, this study proposes a velocity optimization strategy that simultaneously considers powertrain characteristics and battery aging, aiming to jointly enhance fuel economy and battery lifespan. A stacking ensemble-based integrated operating cost model is developed to capture the mapping relationships among vehicle driving state, energy consumption, and battery degradation. This model evaluates the integrated operating cost during ecological velocity optimization, which incorporates both the cost of energy consumption and battery aging. Furthermore, an iterative dynamic programming approach is employed in conjunction with the ensemble learning model to optimize the ecological velocity trajectory by integrating Bellman's optimality principle with the data-driven cost model. The simulation results demonstrate that incorporating powertrain characteristics and battery aging into the PHEV ecological velocity planning facilitates superior speed trajectories, enhanced fuel economy and prolonged battery lifespan under various driving conditions.

title: NCCL-BOT: Closing the Loop on NCCL's Cost Model with Online Bandits
summary: NCCL picks an algorithm-protocol pair for every collective from an analytic cost model (AUTO) that never sees a measured latency. The model is a strong prior but a brittle final decision: priced on forced-arm runs, its choice is exact on most contexts and badly wrong in a few. We built NCCL-BOT, a tuner plugin that closes the loop: a per-context bandit, warm-started from the model, learns from measured latencies. We replay a forced-arm H100 sweep, tuned at 4-8 nodes and scored at 16-32, and price the model's choice on the same forced arms; that sweep has no stock-NCCL run. The bandit cuts the contexts where the model's choice loses more than 10% from 19 to 1 (p99 103% to 9.9%, mean 6.1% to 1.6%; p=0.047 over nine scenarios after Holm correction). The prior and continued learning both matter: cold-started bandits, and committing after one probe of each arm, lose more on the mean in every scenario. Supervised selectors fit once on the same data and tuned with the same budget match the mean, and their heavier tail is not significant (7 against 1 contexts above 10%, p=0.06); at seen scales they match or beat online selection. With hyperparameters frozen from H100, UCB1 cuts AUTO's p99 from 60% to 23% and from 56% to 15% on two GB200 fabrics, but its contexts above 10% go from 16 to 8 on one and from 10 to 13 on the other, and scenario-level tests do not separate the two. Live, on two latency-emulated node sets of one H100 system with one run per policy, the learners repair most of a gross AUTO error on one (selection loss 31% to 6-8% for deterministic Greedy and UCB1; average all-reduce bandwidth 1.18-1.24x stock) but average 0.94-0.99x stock on the other, and on both lose to stock below 1 MiB (on the first through plugin overhead); on H100 the cost model is exact there offline, so small sizes can be left to it. We do not show a net end-to-end win.

title: Cost Optimization of Welded Steel I-Columns Under Eurocode 3 Using Constrained Lagrangian Attention-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Welded steel I-columns are primary load-bearing members in mid- to high-rise structural frames. Their cost-optimal design under code-based limit states is a discrete constrained problem, recently addressed using reinforcement learning. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches either coarsen the action space for centralized decision-making, sacrificing access to the cost-optimal slender-plate regime, or employ parameter-shared multi-agent decompositions that still result in a residual cost gap compared to per-case global optima. To reduce this gap, this study proposes Constrained Lagrangian Attention-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (CLA-MARL), which distributes three components across distinct mechanistic channels of the learning system. A proportional–integral–derivative (PID)-controlled Lagrange multiplier replaces the static feasibility-penalty term and adapts to varying load demand. A cross-attention block with a strict causal mask augments the multi-agent backbone, conditioning each agent on its predecessors. Finally, a cost-first bidirectional refinement procedure replaces greedy shrinkage, exploring paired-variable trades to escape local minima in the weak-axis-governed regime. The framework is formulated under Eurocode 3 over a discrete design space of approximately 1.77 × 107 configurations governed by axial-bending-buckling interaction. On a 130-case benchmark, partitioned into 100 in-distribution and 30 out-of-distribution cases, CLA-MARL recovers the exhaustive global optimum bit-identically on every case across three independent training seeds. This is achieved by combining the trained policy with policy-guided bidirectional refinement. Furthermore, 100% feasibility is maintained for column lengths beyond the training-distribution support.

title: Performance Prediction Techniques for Deep Learning Systems: A Survey
summary: The rapid advancement of deep learning models has led to their widespread application across various domains; however, this has resulted in a significant increase in both hardware and software costs, necessitating optimizations for resource efficiency. To address this issue, performance prediction techniques evaluate the performance impact of corresponding optimizations on deep learning systems to maximize performance gains. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of performance prediction techniques for deep learning systems, categorizing them into allocation, cluster, and accelerator levels based on the system level at which their corresponding optimizations are situated, ranging from high to low. Allocation-level techniques primarily construct the relationships between resource configurations and their performance, cluster-level techniques model the optimizations within deep learning frameworks at given configurations, while accelerator-level techniques assess the efficiency of specific hardware. We point out that prediction techniques at different levels exhibit a hierarchical relationship rather than operating in isolation. High-level prediction techniques can incorporate the results from low-level techniques into their performance models to accommodate more low-level optimizations and improve their prediction accuracy. However, this will slow down the construction and execution speed of performance models, requiring trade-offs for specific use cases. Finally, we discuss future challenges and research directions in performance prediction techniques for deep learning systems.

title: FedKubeRL: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Scheduling and Fault Tolerance in Federated Kubernetes Multi-Clusters
summary: Federated Kubernetes architectures spanning multiple clusters face critical scheduling challenges that require balancing latency, cost, capacity, and fault tolerance. While deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches have shown promise for single-cluster scheduling, they suffer from poor generalization when deployed across heterogeneous multi-cluster environments. We present FedKubeRL, a robust reinforcement learning framework that employs domain randomization during training to achieve cross-cluster generalization. Our approach randomizes node heterogeneity parameters, network latency distributions, and spot instance interruption probabilities. Experimental evaluation using Alibaba Cluster Trace workloads demonstrates that FedKubeRL reduces service-level objective (SLO) violations by 72% and operational costs by 29% compared to the default Kubernetes scheduler. Compared to a DRL baseline without domain randomization, FedKubeRL achieves 29% lower SLO violations and maintains 85% normalized performance on unseen cluster configurations versus 58% for the baseline.

title: Compiler-Hardware Codesign for Deep Learning Acceleration
summary: Deep learning is now deployed at scales ranging from microcontrollers that spot a keyword on a single battery charge to models whose power draw is quoted in units of entire power plants. The efficiency these workloads demand is increasingly delivered by dataflow accelerators: highly parallel, often quantized datapaths, fed from software-managed scratchpads and driven by a host processor. Such accelerators are orders of magnitude more efficient than general-purpose processors, but in practice hard to use. Their programming models are far poorer than those of graphics processing units, and a chip takes years to design while neural network architectures change in months. The result is the hardware lottery: an idea succeeds partly because it fits the hardware that happens to be available and well supported, rather than on its merits alone. Compilers are the natural way out: escaping that lottery means making it cheap to explore combinations of algorithm, soft-and hardware. Production compilers, however, are built around a representation that models a machine as scalar registers, fine-grained instructions and a cache. A dataflow accelerator is none of those things. This thesis therefore asks which hardware primitives and compiler-visible semantics such an accelerator must expose for a compiler to exploit it effectively (the interface question), how a compiler can driveit as close to its theoretical roofline as possible (the performance question), and, when a programmable accelerator and its compiler are generated from one specification, how fast a design iteration becomes and what the design choices this opens up cost in silicon area and in cycles (the cost question). The thesis first argues that these are questions about representation. A compiler can only optimize on the facts its representation states. Applying a standard pipeline of MLIR (multi-level intermediate representation), a widely used compiler framework, to a matrix multiplication produces correct scalar code that uses none of the hardware an accelerator provides, and what that pipeline discards is exactly what an accelerator would have required. On memory, the compiled program does not state in which memory a buffer lives or how its data is laid out, and it contains neither a loop that splits the work into tiles nor the transfers that move those tiles into the accelerator's local memory. Since the weights of realistic networks do not fit in that memory, such a program is not merely slow on the accelerator: it cannot run on it at all. On control, no operation stands for an accelerator invocation, and the configuration one requires has no cost model and is written as volatile stores, a form that forbids the very transformations its cost calls for. On compute, the target is not described in any form the compiler can read, so every accelerator needs a backend built for it alone. Three contributions close these gaps in turn, moving from a fixed accelerator to a generated one. HTVM, a deep learning compiler, addresses memory on a fixed heterogeneous system-on-chip, combining a graph-level pattern matcher with a tiling solver that sizes tiles to fit the accelerator's local memory and keeps transfers contiguous. It deploys the full MLPerf Tiny benchmark suite on the DIANA chip and reaches one to two orders of magnitude over running on its processor alone, at a runtime overhead measured rather than assumed: a few percent on convolutions, against 54.5% on the fastest fully connected layer, where too few compute cycles are available to hide the setup work. title: BECON: Belief-Conditioned Constrained Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning under Drifting Preferences and Budgets
summary: Constrained preference-conditioned MORL typically assumes full task observability, treating preferences and safety budgets as stationary task signals. In real-world deployment, however, these signals are often unreliable proxies: intent may drift, safety tolerances may shift with context, and exposed descriptors may be noisy, delayed, or incomplete. We therefore formulate constrained preference-conditioned MORL as a partially observed task-specification problem, where the agent must navigate a fundamental conflict between unreliable external signals and latent interaction dynamics. We propose \textbf{BECON}, a belief-conditioned framework for constrained MORL with drifting preferences and budgets, which infers latent task context from recent histories to estimate preferences and safety budgets. These estimates are fused with the exposed task signal via uncertainty-dependent gates, enabling the policy to defer to observations under high epistemic uncertainty while correcting them when history is informative. The fused context jointly conditions preference optimization and context-adaptive constraint enforcement. Experiments on diverse multi-objective control tasks demonstrate that BECON consistently improves over state-of-the-art MORL baselines, achieving stronger robustness and constraint satisfaction under task drift.

title: Policy-Based Resolution of Vendor Indeterminate States in Card-Not-Present Fraud Orchestration at Production Scale
summary: Merchants increasingly buy fraud risk assessment from commercial scoring services rather than building it, and those services commonly return three values: approve, decline, or review. The third value is indeterminate rather than adverse, because it reports that the vendor model cannot separate the transaction on its own evidence. What a merchant does with that third value is unconstrained by the vendor, yet the orchestration literature reviewed here treats it as a work item for human adjudication, assessed by how small the resulting queue becomes. Whether automated resolution is preferable, and under what conditions, has not been reported from a production deployment at scale. This paper documents and analyses a production alternative in which the indeterminate state is resolved principally by merchant policy evaluated against context the scoring vendor does not observe, including account tenure, chargeback history, payment geography, and merchant-maintained identifier lists. The deployment is formalised as a five-principle orchestration pattern; the merchant policy layer, the authentication path, and the data-protection boundary are described as documented at extraction; and the complete operational export of an anonymised multi-vertical card-not-present platform is analysed, covering 736,707 authorization records from January 2020 to September 2026. A three-policy cost model then states the conditions under which proceeding, declining, or adjudicating minimises expected cost at a given fraud prevalence. Of all orders, 53.25 percent were approved, 10.23 percent declined, and 36.52 percent entered the indeterminate state. Of that indeterminate population, 95.41 percent were resolved to approve and 2.24 percent to decline by policy, while 2.34 percent were routed to an internal manual process, so 99.14 percent of all orders reached a terminal disposition without manual adjudication. Attribution separated 11,280 platform-policy declines from 64,097 processor-side refusals, showing that aggregate merchant decline rates overstate fraud-policy intervention by a factor of approximately 6.68. Policy resolution is therefore an explicit architectural and economic decision rather than a default; it bounds rather than eliminates human adjudication; and decline rates reported without attribution are not comparable across deployments. The study characterises operating behaviour and does not evaluate fraud-detection effectiveness, because matured transaction-level fraud labels were unavailable.

title: Technology Transition at an Existing Porphyry Copper Mine: Concentration, Primary-Sulfide Hydrometallurgy, and Pilot Learning
summary: Existing porphyry copper mines often face a transition from a depleting oxide operation to a known sulfide inventory. The mature alternative is concentration and flotation, whereas direct-ore primary-sulfide hydrometallurgy remains uncertain at commercial scale. This paper advances mining investment and processing research by integrating four elements that have previously been treated separately: remaining oxide life as an option-preserving operating buffer; finite-inventory, engineering-constrained selection of route and capacity; an explicit distinction among the installed oxide route, mature concentration, direct-ore hydrometallurgy, and concentration followed by concentrate hydrometallurgy; and an industrial pilot valued as a Bayesian scale-transfer experiment. The resulting finite-horizon real-options model uses one risk-adjusted mean-reverting copper-price process before and after investment and incorporates ramp-up, availability, residence time, water, power, tailings or residue capacity, and asset compatibility. Four propositions establish unique conditional capacity, local exercise-boundary geometry, the conditions under which pilot information has decision value, and the value and regularity effects of the oxide-depletion deadline. These results clarify why a route boundary may become steep, disappear, or diverge, and why technically precise testing can be economically worthless when it does not change route, timing, or scale. In a reproducible synthetic case centered on USD 14,000/t Cu, the preferred action moves from concentration to piloting and then to direct-ore hydrometallurgy as commercial-performance confidence rises. The contribution is a transferable stage-gated decision rule, not a universal price trigger, technology endorsement, feasibility study, or reserve declaration.

title: AI-Driven Robotic Path Planning and Adaptive Motion Control for Collaborative Construction Automation in Unstructured Building Environments
summary: Unstructured building environments impose coupled challenges for construction robots: cluttered and partially observed workspaces, changing task sequences, uncertain material placement, contact-rich manipulation, and the need to share space safely with workers and other machines. This manuscript develops a methodological framework for AI-driven robotic path planning and adaptive motion control in collaborative construction automation. The central contribution is an integrated formulation that links probabilistic workspace representation, risk-aware path planning, impedance-based motion control, uncertainty-aware policy adaptation, and multi-robot task allocation within a single safety-constrained decision architecture. The framework treats construction sites as dynamic stochastic environments in which geometric occupancy, prediction uncertainty, human proximity, and task precedence jointly determine admissible motion. Planning is expressed as a risk-regularized optimization problem, while control adapts stiffness, damping, and reference trajectories in response to contact conditions and collaboration signals. The analysis specifies how uncertainty affects exploration, path feasibility, and safety margins, and it identifies the conditions under which learning should tune high-level parameters rather than direct actuator commands. An evaluation logic is proposed for separating planning, control, coordination, and adaptation effects through targeted ablations and safety-envelope analysis. The framework provides a technically defensible basis for deploying collaborative construction robots without treating site uncertainty as an exceptional condition.
